missBART

Website and documentation: https://andrewcparnell.github.io/missBART/

Joint models for multivariate responses with non-ignorable missing values, built on Bayesian additive regression trees (BART).

The responses follow a multivariate BART model. The missingness indicators follow a model in which the responses themselves are predictors, so that data missing completely at random, missing at random and missing not at random (MNAR) can all be handled, and the missing responses are imputed while the model is fitted:

Function Model for the missingness
missBART1() multivariate probit regression on (1, x, y)
missBART2() multivariate probit BART on (x, y)
mvBART() none: multivariate BART for complete responses

The methods are described in

Goh, Y. C., Soh, W. K., Parnell, A. C. and Murphy, K. (2024). Joint models for handling non-ignorable missing data using Bayesian additive regression trees: application to leaf photosynthetic traits data. arXiv:2412.14946

Installation

The samplers are written in C++ (Rcpp and RcppArmadillo), so a C++ toolchain is needed to install from source (Rtools on Windows, Xcode command line tools on macOS).

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("yongchengoh/missBART")

Example 

library(missBART)

set.seed(1)
n <- 500
x <- matrix(runif(n * 5), ncol = 5)
y_true <- cbind(10 * sin(pi * x[, 1] * x[, 2]) + 10 * x[, 4], 5 * x[, 1] - 8 * x[, 2]^2) +
  matrix(rnorm(2 * n), ncol = 2)

# large values are more likely to be missing
y <- y_true
y[runif(n) < pnorm(-1 + scale(y_true[, 1])), 1] <- NA
y[runif(n) < pnorm(-1 + scale(y_true[, 2])), 2] <- NA

fit1 <- missBART1(x, y)                      # probit regression missingness model
fit2 <- missBART2(x, y, n_class_trees = 20)  # probit BART missingness model

fit1
head(imputed_values(fit1))   # posterior summaries of the missing responses
y_complete <- completed_data(fit1)
coef(fit1)                   # probit coefficients: positive = more likely to be missing
varimp(fit2)                 # which predictors the missingness trees split on

vignette("missBART") has a longer walk-through, and the package website has further articles, including a re-run of the simulation studies in the paper. Scripts for the simulations and the application in the paper are in Examples/.

Speed

Version 0.2.0 moved the samplers from R to C++. Seconds per 1,000 MCMC iterations on simulated MNAR data with five covariates, 100 regression trees and (for missBART2) 20 missingness trees, single core:

n responses model 0.1.0 (R) 0.2.0 (C++) speed-up
500 1 missBART1 95 0.57 170x
500 1 missBART2 110 0.63 170x
500 1 mvBART 86 0.48 180x
2000 2 missBART1 1043 3.0 350x
2000 2 missBART2 248 2.9 90x
2000 2 mvBART 186 2.1 90x
2000 5 missBART1 1553 5.4 290x
2000 5 missBART2 389 5.0 80x
2000 5 mvBART 304 3.5 90x

The C++ timings are averages over 5,000 iterations. The R timings are averages over the first 50 iterations only, when the trees are still small, so they flatter the R code. At these rates the 10,000 iterations used in the paper for n = 2000 and five responses take about 55 seconds with missBART1, instead of about 4.3 hours. Examples/benchmark.R reproduces the table.

Running both versions for the same 2,000 iterations on one simulated data set (n = 500, two responses) gave:

model time 0.1.0 time 0.2.0 imputation RMSE 0.1.0 imputation RMSE 0.2.0
missBART1 621 s 1.7 s 1.24 1.17
missBART2 246 s 1.5 s 1.16 1.11
mvBART 196 s 1.1 s – –

The two versions do not produce identical draws for the same seed, and a few steps of the sampler were changed; see NEWS.md.
